title: Message Submission for Mail
summary: Splits message submission from message relay, so each can follow its own rules for security and policy, and specifies what a submission server should do. Relay and final delivery continue to use SMTP on port 25, while submission normally uses port 587. It was a draft standard that obsoleted RFC 2476, and was replaced by RFC 6409.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending your own mail and passing mail along between post offices are different jobs. This gives them separate doors, with your own letters going in through door 587.

questions: what is a message submission agent
subtitle: Why mail clients should hand outgoing mail to a separate submission server, normally on port 587.

tldr.problem: SMTP was designed to transfer finished messages, but it is also used to submit new ones, and submission needs authentication, authorization and sometimes message fixes that relay should not do.
tldr.mechanism: Submission is split from relay. A Message Submission Agent accepts mail from mail clients, normally on port 587, and must require authentication and fully qualified domains, with recommended and optional checks and message fixes.
tldr.outcome: Relay and final delivery stay on SMTP port 25. The RFC obsoleted RFC 2476 and has been obsoleted by RFC 6409.

today: RFC 4409 was a Draft Standard that obsoleted RFC 2476, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 6409.

sections.title: Why Split Submission From Relay
sections.content:
SMTP was defined to transfer finished messages, and Message Transfer Agents (MTAs) are not supposed to alter message text beyond adding trace fields. But SMTP is also widely used so that Message User Agents (MUAs), the mail clients, can introduce new messages. The process that accepts them is a Message Submission Agent (MSA).

Relay is often unauthenticated, but authentication of submissions has become more important. Many sites prohibit outbound traffic on port 25 because of machines with worms or viruses that send spam, and funnel submissions through submission servers. Submitted messages may also be unfinished, for example missing a proper Date field or with domains not fully qualified, and fixes made by downstream MTAs have been shown to cause harm.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail from your own computer should go through a front desk that checks who you are and tidies the envelope, instead of the mail sorting room.

sections.title: Port 587 and Authorized Submission
sections.content:
Port 587 is reserved for message submission, and messages arriving there are defined to be submissions. The protocol is ESMTP with extra restrictions and allowances. A site MAY instead use port 25 by designating some hosts as MSAs and others as MTAs.

The RFC discusses ways to authorize submitters: authenticated SMTP, IP address restrictions, secure IP and other tunnels, and prior POP authentication. Authenticated SMTP has seen widespread deployment. IP restrictions do not suit travelers and can be spoofed. The POP method has a window in which an unauthorized user may appear to be an authorized one.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk has its own door, number 587. There are several ways it can check who you are, and a password check is the most common.

sections.title: What an MSA Must, Should and May Do
sections.content:
An MSA MUST ensure all domains in the SMTP envelope are fully qualified, and must do the same in address header fields if it examines or alters the text. It MUST by default give an error to MAIL if the session is not authenticated with SMTP AUTH, unless authentication or authorization is already established, for example inside a protected subnetwork. Code 554 rejects improper commands, and 530 is used for missing authentication.

An MSA SHOULD reject illegal address syntax (code 501 for an improper address) and SHOULD log errors, with limits on logging to prevent denial of service. It MAY enforce submission rights and permissions (code 550, such as enhanced code 5.7.1), check message data, and allow reduced authentication for mail to the postmaster address, so users can report problems that prevent submitting mail.

If the MSA cannot determine a return path, it SHOULD reject immediately with 550 to the MAIL command. A null return path (MAIL FROM:<>) alone MUST NOT be a reason to reject. For most other rejections the MSA MAY accept and then send a bounce, but immediate rejection is preferred because it gives direct feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk must check you are allowed in and that every address is complete. It should reject badly written addresses, and it may do extra checks if the site wants.

sections.title: Interaction With SMTP Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC lists SMTP extensions with a requirement level on the submission port. AUTH MUST be supported. PIPELINING, ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, DSN and 8BITMIME are SHOULD. ETRN and the 521 reply code MUST NOT be used. SIZE, CHECKPOINT, BINARYMIME, CHUNKING, STARTTLS, NO-SOLICITING and MTRK are MAY.

Enhanced status codes let the MSA explain problems in more detail, but care is needed not to expose more detail than necessary to unauthenticated senders. Future SMTP extensions SHOULD say whether they are valid on the submission port.
sections.plainLanguage: Some extra features are required at the front desk, some are encouraged and a few are banned.

sections.title: Message Modifications
sections.content:
Sites MAY modify submissions to meet standards and site policy, but should limit changes to specific problems with clear fixes. Indiscriminately appending a domain to an address usually produces more broken addresses. Anything the MSA forwards MUST still conform to the SMTP and message format standards.

Permitted changes include adding or replacing Sender, adding or correcting Date, adding Message-ID (a SHOULD), applying MIME transfer encoding, signing, encrypting, resolving aliases and rewriting headers per local policy. The MSA MUST NOT rewrite a destination address in a way that violates SMTP limits on changing local-parts. Signing or encrypting is only useful if the connection between MUA and MSA is itself secured.
sections.plainLanguage: The front desk may fix small mistakes on your envelope, like a missing date. It should only fix things it is sure about.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
Separating submission from relay lets a site apply different policies to each, including extra security, in a way that is simpler to do correctly. A site could require authentication at the MSA and have the MTA reject RCPT commands for non-local users. A site that requires no authorization for submissions allows open use of its resources and name, and unsolicited bulk email can be injected through it.

For IANA, the registration for port 587 now refers to this memo instead of RFC 2476.
sections.plainLanguage: Having separate doors makes it easier to guard each one properly. A door that lets anyone in will get used by spammers.

viz.caption: REPLY CODES NAMED FOR MSA REJECTIONS

items.label: Authentication needed
items.desc: Used when the session has not been authenticated.

items.label: Improper command
items.desc: General rejection of MAIL, RCPT or DATA, including improper domains.

items.label: Bad address syntax
items.desc: Detectably improper address in MAIL or RCPT.

items.label: Not permitted
items.desc: No return path, or insufficient rights or permissions.
